skill.title: Define stratified, cluster and quota sampling; role of randomisation and controls
skill.output: method; biases, limitations, ethics; control group
skill.example: sampling by year group proportionally → stratified
needs: Select a simple random sample and spot bias
Identify surveys, observational studies and designed experiments

steps.title: Split the students into two groups

lines.text: Stratified sampling takes a sample from each group in proportion to its size. Here the groups are students with a pet and students without a pet.
Each group is 50% of the students, so each should make up 50% of the sample.

steps.title: Work out the size of each sample

lines.text: Take a random sample of 1260 from all the students in country Z who have a pet.
Take a random sample of 1260 from all the students in country Z who do not have a pet.

steps.title: Why this is probably not useful

lines.text: There is probably no connection between owning a pet and maths scores, so splitting by pet ownership gives no better estimate of the scores.

references.final: \text{Random sample of 1260 pet owners and 1260 non-owners; pet ownership is probably unrelated to maths scores}

skill.title: Explain the effect of outliers on summary statistics
skill.example: removing 30 lowers the mean much more than the median

steps.title: Say how the mean is affected

lines.text: Making the biggest number bigger increases the total (sum) of the 10 numbers.
The mean is the total divided by 10, so the mean increases as well.

steps.title: Say how the median is affected

lines.text: For 10 numbers the median depends only on the middle two values, the 5th and 6th biggest.
The biggest number is the 10th, so changing it does not change the 5th or 6th values. The median stays the same.
Tick the box for the mean only.

skill.title: Analyse plots to explain differences in centre and spread
needs: Compare data sets with back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots

steps.title: Compare the spread on each side of the plot

lines.text: Before exercise the rates run from $60$ to $89$, a range of $29$.
After exercise they run from $71$ to $118$, a range of $47$.
The after-exercise values are more spread out, so the standard deviation increased.

references.final: \text{Increased: there is a greater spread in the data}
